# MEMORANDUM

**To:** [Supervising Partner]
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 10, 2026
**Re:** Trouseind / Reitaisk: acquisition of Cobbelly Inflight Kitchens, Inc.: issues across the deal package

**Privileged & Confidential: Attorney Work Product**

---

## I. Summary

I reviewed the five documents in the matter folder:

- the February 2026 draft Stock Purchase Agreement (**SPA**);
- the Escrow Agreement with Lanterwick Trust Company, N.A. (**Escrow Agreement**);
- the Transition Services Agreement (**TSA**);
- Seller's February 20, 2026 draft side letter on tax survival (**Side Letter**); and
- Pembury & Vane's insurance certificate cover letter.

The SPA is broadly buyer-protective. It has:

- New York law (§11.8);
- an exclusive New York County forum covering all Transaction Documents (§11.9);
- an 18-month general survival period;
- statute-of-limitations-plus-60-days survival for the Seller Fundamental Representations and for tax; and
- a $3,000,000 Extended Holdback that secures the Fundamental Representations and Pre-Closing Taxes.

The ancillary documents undercut that protection in five places. Two features of the SPA make them more damaging:

- **The Escrow Agreement controls escrow payouts.** SPA §11.10 says the SPA prevails over the other Transaction Documents, *except that the Escrow Agreement governs disbursement of the Escrow Funds*. Wherever the Escrow Agreement differs from the SPA on who gets paid from escrow, the Escrow Agreement wins.
- **The Escrow Agent will not look past its own document.** Escrow Agreement §6.1 says Lanterwick is not bound by or charged with notice of the SPA.

The issues are ranked below by significance to the client:

| # | Issue | Location | Type of fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Trouseind gives Reitaisk an **uncapped indemnity covering Reitaisk's own negligence** in meal production | TSA §§8.1, 9.2 | Drafting change, plus a business decision on risk allocation |
| 2 | The Extended Holdback **does not secure Tax (3.14) or Food Safety (3.17) claims** | Escrow Agreement §§1.1, 5.3 (via SPA §11.10) | Drafting change |
| 3 | Tax survival is cut to **9 months**, ending before Seller's 2026 return is even due | Side Letter §2 | Reject (business confirmation) |
| 4 | **Delaware law and exclusive Chancery forum** for escrow disputes, against New York for everything else | Escrow Agreement §10.2 | Drafting change (possible Escrow Agent negotiation) |
| 5 | **Reitaisk may assign or delegate the TSA to anyone**, including a competitor, without consent | TSA §12.3 | Drafting change |

The insurance cover letter does not raise a drafting issue. Some related diligence points are in Part III.

---

## II. Issues (in order of priority)

### 1. Uncapped indemnity by Trouseind for Reitaisk's own negligence

**Location:** TSA §8.1 (Indemnification by Recipient), read with §9.2 (Cap). Related provisions: §8.2, §9.1 and §7.1.

**What the documents say:**

- **§8.1 (Trouseind's indemnity).** Trouseind, as Recipient, must indemnify, defend and hold harmless the Provider Indemnitees against "all Losses arising out of or relating to the provision or receipt of the Services, *including any negligence of Provider*." The only exception is Losses that Provider must itself indemnify under §8.2.
- **§8.2 (Reitaisk's indemnity).** Reitaisk indemnifies only for its own **gross negligence or willful misconduct**.
- **§9.2 (cap).** Each party's aggregate liability is capped at the TSA Fees, "*other than Article VIII* obligations." Trouseind's §8.1 indemnity therefore has no cap.
- **§9.1 (damages exclusion).** The exclusion of consequential damages and lost profits does not apply to amounts payable to third parties under Article VIII.

**Why it matters to Trouseind:**

- **Who bears the risk.** The Meal Production Services are Reitaisk producing meals at its own Milwaukee Commissary, with its own staff, under its own food safety plan (TSA §§2.3, 2.5). Contamination, foreign-object, temperature-excursion and undeclared-allergen incidents are the central risks of airline catering. Third-party claims from passengers, airline customers and regulators can be very large.
- **The gap between §8.1 and §8.2.** Under the draft, a passenger illness caused by Reitaisk's *ordinary* negligence in Milwaukee is not caught by §8.2. It falls into §8.1. Trouseind would defend and pay Reitaisk's losses, without limit.
- **New York will likely enforce it.** The TSA is governed by New York law (TSA §13.2), consistent with SPA §11.8. New York courts enforce an agreement to indemnify a party for its own negligence where that intent is unmistakably clear from the language. The words "including any negligence of Provider" are about as clear as such language gets. We should not expect a court to rescue Trouseind on public policy or construction grounds.
- **Reitaisk has little incentive to take care.** Its own exposure to Trouseind for defective performance is capped at the TSA Fees (§9.2), and it is indemnified for its ordinary negligence. Its incentive to maintain food safety discipline during the transition is weak, at exactly the period when Cobbelly's customer relationships are most fragile.
- **Insurance does not close the gap.** TSA §7.1 requires Reitaisk to carry CGL, recall and umbrella insurance and to name Trouseind and the Company as additional insureds. That insurance is undercut because the contractual indemnity runs the wrong way. Reitaisk's insurers may also look to Trouseind's indemnity through subrogation or contractual-liability arguments.

**Recommended fix:**

- **Rewrite §8.1.** Trouseind should indemnify only for Losses arising from (a) Recipient's or the Company's own negligence, willful misconduct or breach of the TSA, and (b) Customer Specifications furnished by Recipient or the Company that were inaccurate, to the extent Provider followed them. Delete "including any negligence of Provider." Add an express statement that Recipient has no obligation for Losses caused by Provider's negligence.
- **Broaden §8.2.** Reitaisk should indemnify for Losses arising from:
  - Provider's negligence (not only gross negligence) or willful misconduct;
  - breach of the TSA, including §2.2 (standard of performance) and §2.3 (food safety program);
  - violation of Food Safety Laws; and
  - any contamination, adulteration, foreign-object, allergen or recall event affecting meals produced at the Milwaukee Commissary, except to the extent caused by Recipient-supplied specifications.
- **Restructure §9.2.**
  - Bring Recipient's §8.1 indemnity under a cap.
  - Leave Provider's §8.2 indemnity for third-party food safety claims uncapped, or capped at a meaningful figure that is at least the required insurance limits.
  - Make Provider's direct liability cap (currently the Fees) higher for food safety breaches.

**Business decision for the client:** Trouseind should decide how far it is prepared to go on risk allocation for the transition period. For example:

- whether it will accept any cap on Reitaisk's food safety indemnity, and at what level; and
- whether it wants Reitaisk's insurance limits under §7.1 increased.

For reference, the Company's own umbrella limit is $15,000,000 and its recall limit is $5,000,000. Reitaisk's required limits are $10,000,000 umbrella and $2,000,000 recall. The opening drafting position should be the mutual, fault-based structure above.

---

### 2. Extended Holdback does not secure Tax (3.14) or Food Safety (3.17) claims

**Location:** Escrow Agreement §1.1 (definition of "Fundamental Representation Claims") and §5.3(a)–(b). These conflict with SPA §1.1 ("Seller Fundamental Representations"), §2.4 and §9.6(b). SPA §11.10 decides which prevails.

**What the documents say:**

- **The SPA.** SPA §1.1 defines the Seller Fundamental Representations as §§3.1, 3.2, 3.3, **3.14 (Taxes)** and **3.17 (Food Safety and Regulatory Compliance)**. SPA §2.4 provides that the $3,000,000 Extended Holdback secures claims for breach of the Seller Fundamental Representations *and* for Pre-Closing Taxes under §9.2(c). SPA §9.6(b) follows the same approach.
- **The Escrow Agreement.** Escrow Agreement §1.1 defines "Fundamental Representation Claims" as Claims for breach of "*Sections 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3 of the Purchase Agreement*" only. Escrow Agreement §5.3(a) makes the Extended Holdback available "solely for Fundamental Representation Claims." It bars the Escrow Agent from paying any other Claim from the holdback. Escrow Agreement §5.3(b) limits the amount retained at the Extended Release Date to pending Fundamental Representation Claims.
- **Which controls.** SPA §11.10 provides that the SPA prevails over other Transaction Documents, *except that the Escrow Agreement governs the disbursement of the Escrow Funds*. Under Escrow Agreement §6.1, Lanterwick is not bound by or charged with notice of the SPA. The narrower escrow definition will therefore control what Lanterwick actually pays.

**Why it matters to Trouseind:**

- **Long-tail claims lose their security.** Tax and food safety are the two long-tail risks in this deal.
  - Tax deficiencies surface on audit, often years after closing.
  - Food safety claims include regulatory findings, recalls and latent incident history that SPA §3.17(d) was meant to capture.
- **Recovery becomes an unsecured claim after month 12.** The General Escrow Amount ($5,640,000) is released at the 12-month Initial Release Date. After that, the only security left is the $3,000,000 Extended Holdback, and Lanterwick could not pay any 3.14, 3.17 or §9.2(c) Pre-Closing Tax claim from it. Trouseind would have to pursue Reitaisk directly as an unsecured creditor.
- **The holdback ends up protecting the least likely claims.** The holdback would cover only organization, authority and capitalization. Those are the representations least likely to be breached and the easiest to diligence. Under the draft, $3,000,000 of the purchase price stays in escrow for three years largely without serving its commercial purpose.

**Recommended fix:**

- **Fix the definition.** Amend Escrow Agreement §1.1 so that "Fundamental Representation Claims" means Claims for (a) any inaccuracy in or breach of the *Seller Fundamental Representations (as defined in the Purchase Agreement)*, and (b) indemnification for Pre-Closing Taxes under SPA §9.2(c). Cross-referring to the SPA definition, rather than repeating section numbers, prevents the two documents from drifting apart again.
- **Conform §5.1(a) and §5.3** to the revised definition.
- **Add a back-stop in SPA §11.10.** Provide that defined terms used in the Escrow Agreement have the meanings given in the SPA, and that the Escrow Agreement's control of disbursement does not narrow the categories of claims secured under SPA §2.4.

This is a drafting point. Seller agreed the commercial deal in SPA §2.4, and we should present it as conforming the Escrow Agreement to that deal.

---

### 3. Side Letter cuts tax survival to nine months, ending before the pre-closing tax return is filed

**Location:** Side Letter §2 (§2.1, replacing SPA §9.1(b); §2.3, fixing the Closing Date reference). The current position is in SPA §9.1(b), §9.2(c) and §6.8(a).

**What the documents say:**

- **Current SPA position.** SPA §9.1(b) provides that the §3.14 Tax representations and the §9.2(c) Pre-Closing Taxes indemnity survive until **60 days after the applicable statute of limitations expires**, including any waiver or extension.
- **Seller's proposal.** The Side Letter is framed as an amendment under SPA §11.6. It would replace §9.1(b) so that both survive only "until the date that is *nine (9) months after the Closing Date*."
- **Resulting date.** Based on the March 31, 2026 Closing Date in SPA §3.1(c), which Side Letter §2.3 expressly adopts, survival ends on **December 31, 2026**.
- **When the return is due.** Under SPA §6.8(a), Seller files the Seller Group's consolidated federal income Tax Return for the year ending December 31, 2026. That return includes the Company through the end of the Closing Date. For a calendar-year group, it is not due until **April 15, 2027**, or **October 15, 2027** if extended.

**Why it matters to Trouseind:**

- **Survival would end before the risk arises.** It would expire before the main pre-closing return for the stub period is filed. It would also expire well before the IRS or any state could audit that return or the Company's earlier years.
- **Claims must be made within survival.** Under SPA §9.1(d), a claim is preserved only if it is asserted in writing, with reasonable specificity, before survival expires. As a practical matter, Trouseind could not assert a tax claim in time.
- **Consolidated-return exposure goes unprotected.** Pre-Closing Taxes (SPA §1.1) expressly include several liability under Treas. Reg. §1.1502-6 for the whole Seller Group's consolidated tax. This exposure belongs to Reitaisk's group, but the Company carries it after closing. Trouseind can neither control nor diligence it. Since 2019 the Company has been part of that group (SPA §3.14(e)).
- **The proposal is internally inconsistent.** The Extended Holdback runs for three years (SPA §2.4(b)) precisely to secure long-tail claims, including Pre-Closing Taxes. A nine-month survival period would empty it of tax coverage.

**Status:** The Side Letter is a Seller draft. It is marked "not binding unless and until executed by both parties" and has not been countersigned. Nothing has been conceded.

**Recommended fix:**

- Reject the Side Letter and keep SPA §9.1(b) as drafted: statute of limitations plus 60 days, giving effect to waivers and extensions.
- If Seller is trying to address a specific concern, such as open-ended exposure on a particular tax, address it with a targeted covenant or specific indemnity, not a general cut in survival.
- Under no circumstances should survival end before the statute of limitations on the Seller Group's 2026 consolidated return. That limitations period runs, in general, three years after filing, so into 2030.

**Business decision for the client:** Please confirm the client wants to reject outright. That is my recommendation. We should also confirm that no business-level concession on tax survival was traded for price or another point.

---

### 4. Escrow Agreement chooses Delaware law and an exclusive Delaware Chancery forum, conflicting with the SPA

**Location:** Escrow Agreement §10.2. This conflicts with SPA §11.8 (governing law) and SPA §11.9 (forum). The Escrow Agreement's definition of "Final Order" in §1.1 and §§6.5 and 8.3 also refer back to §10.2. SPA §11.10 decides which prevails.

**What the documents say:**

- **The SPA.** SPA §11.8 provides that the SPA, and all claims relating to it or the transactions it contemplates, are **governed by New York law**. SPA §11.9 requires all proceedings arising out of the SPA *or any other Transaction Document* to be brought exclusively in the state or federal courts in **New York County**. The Escrow Agreement is a Transaction Document. The TSA follows the same approach (TSA §§13.2, 13.3).
- **The Escrow Agreement.** Escrow Agreement §10.2 instead applies "the *laws of the State of Delaware*." It gives the "*Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware*" exclusive jurisdiction over any dispute about the disbursement of, or entitlement to, the Escrow Funds, *including whether a Claim is valid*. It falls back to the Delaware Superior Court or the District of Delaware.
- **Which controls.** Because SPA §11.10 lets the Escrow Agreement govern disbursement of the Escrow Funds, Seller can argue that the Delaware clause controls escrow disputes.

**Why it matters to Trouseind:**

- **Two forums for one dispute.** For any contested indemnity claim, Trouseind may have to prove Seller's breach and Losses in New York, and separately fight over release of the escrow in Delaware. This means duplicative litigation cost, a risk of inconsistent rulings, and delay.
- **Seller gains leverage.** The Escrow Funds are Trouseind's first-recourse security (SPA §9.6). Seller could object to every Claim Notice and force a Delaware proceeding on validity, delaying recovery while the escrow sits frozen.
- **A New York judgment may not release the funds.** Lanterwick may release contested amounts only on Joint Written Instructions or a "Final Order" (Escrow Agreement §5.1(d), §5.4). "Final Order" is defined as an order of a court "of competent jurisdiction *under Section 10.2*," meaning a Delaware court. A New York County judgment in Trouseind's favor on the merits might therefore not trigger disbursement. Trouseind would then need Seller's cooperation on Joint Written Instructions, or a second, Delaware judgment.
- **The Chancery forum may not work for money claims.** Chancery's equity jurisdiction over a pure contractual money claim is limited. That is presumably why §10.2 includes a fallback, but it adds a threshold jurisdictional fight.

**Recommended fix:**

- **Conform §10.2 to the SPA.** Provide for New York law and the exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts in New York County.
- **Amend "Final Order"** to mean a final, non-appealable order of a court of competent jurisdiction under SPA §11.9.
- **Make the same change in §§6.5 and 8.3** (interpleader and successor appointment).

If Lanterwick insists on Delaware law for its own duties and liabilities, which some escrow agents require as policy, the fallback is a split clause:

- Delaware law may govern only the Escrow Agent's rights, duties and immunities;
- all disputes between Buyer and Seller over entitlement to the Escrow Funds, including Claim validity, are governed by New York law and resolved exclusively in New York County; and
- the Escrow Agent must honor a final New York judgment.

**Possible question for the client:** Trouseind is a Delaware corporation. If it has an affirmative preference for Delaware across the whole package, the alternative is to move the SPA to Delaware too. Whichever is chosen, the documents should be aligned. I assume the client does not want to reopen the SPA's New York choice.

---

### 5. Reitaisk may assign or delegate the TSA to anyone without Trouseind's consent

**Location:** TSA §12.3 (Assignment). Related provisions: TSA §12.2 (production only at the Milwaukee Commissary), §6.1 (confidentiality) and SPA §6.2 (non-compete).

**What the documents say:** TSA §12.3 bars Trouseind from assigning or delegating without Reitaisk's consent. It then provides that "*Provider may assign* or delegate this Agreement, or any of its rights or obligations hereunder, in whole or in part, to any Person without the consent of Recipient."

**Why it matters to Trouseind:**

- **Production could pass to a competitor.** Meal production for Cobbelly's airline customers could be handed to:
  - an unvetted subcontractor;
  - the buyer of the Milwaukee Commissary; or
  - a competing airline caterer.
- **Sensitive information would follow.** The assignee would receive the Company's Confidential Information under the TSA, including menus, recipes, Customer Specifications, pricing, volumes, flight schedules and Airline Customer contacts (TSA §1.1). That would put Cobbelly's most valuable commercial information in a competitor's hands during the transition, when customer relationships are most exposed.
- **It undermines the non-compete.** SPA §6.2 carves out performance of the TSA from Seller's non-compete. A third-party assignee is not bound by SPA §6.2 at all.
- **The site restriction may not hold.** TSA §12.2 restricts production to the Milwaukee Commissary. An assignment "in whole or in part" to "any Person" invites the argument that the assignee may perform elsewhere.
- **Trouseind would be left without remedies.**
  - Trouseind would have no consent right.
  - It would have no termination right specific to a change of provider. The §11.1 convenience termination needs 30 days' notice, which may be too slow if a competitor takes over.
  - It may lose the benefit of Reitaisk's covenant and insurance package if Reitaisk is released.
- **The provision is one-sided.** It is inconsistent with SPA §11.4, under which Seller needs Buyer's consent to assign.

**Recommended fix:**

- **Make §12.3 mutual.** Neither party may assign or delegate without the other's prior written consent.
- **Preserve Trouseind's flexibility.** Trouseind should be free, without consent, to assign to the Company, to Affiliates, to a successor to the Business, or collaterally to lenders, consistent with SPA §11.4.
- **Bar assignment to competitors.** Prohibit any assignment, delegation or subcontracting by Provider to a Person engaged in inflight catering, consent notwithstanding.
- **Keep Reitaisk on the hook.** Any permitted assignment by Provider should not release Reitaisk, and the assignee should assume Articles VI and VIII in writing.
- **Give Trouseind an exit.** Trouseind should have a right to terminate, on short notice and without penalty, on any assignment or change of control of Provider, or any change in the facility or operator performing the Meal Production Services. Provider should owe full migration assistance under §5.3 in that case.
- **Close the subcontracting route.** Expressly prohibit subcontracting of Meal Production Services without consent, tying into §12.2.

---

## III. Other observations (lower priority / diligence)

**Insurance cover letter (Pembury & Vane, February 24, 2026).** This is informational and raises no drafting issue. The certificates "confer no rights" (§4.1), so we should rely on the policies themselves, available through the data room, and the five-year loss runs. Three points to note:

- **These are the Company's policies, not Reitaisk's.** Meals produced at Reitaisk's Milwaukee Commissary under the TSA will be insured, if at all, under Reitaisk's own program. We should require certificates for the TSA §7.1 insurance at signing or closing, not only on the Effective Date. Those certificates should name Trouseind and the Company as additional insureds, on a primary and non-contributory basis with a waiver of subrogation. This links to Issue 1.
- **Policy renewal.** All Company policies renew July 1, 2026. Trouseind should confirm how the Company program was renewed, or moved onto Trouseind's program, after closing. The Company's CGL limits ($2,000,000 per occurrence / $4,000,000 aggregate) are lower than those Reitaisk must carry under TSA §7.1(a) ($5,000,000).
- **SPA §3.18.** The schedule of policies should be checked against the seven policies listed in the letter.

**TSA cap on Reitaisk's direct liability.** Apart from Issue 1, TSA §9.2 caps Reitaisk's direct liability for failed or defective performance at the TSA Fees. If the Milwaukee volumes are significant, the client should consider whether that is adequate, which is a business call. If not, we should seek a higher cap for breaches of §§2.2(c), 2.3 and 2.4.

---

## IV. Questions on deal background

1. **Timing.** The drafts are dated February 2026, with a March 31, 2026 target Closing Date and a May 29, 2026 outside date (SPA §8.1(b)). Please confirm the current status and expected Closing Date. The survival analysis in Issue 3 and the insurance renewal point both depend on dates. If closing has moved, the dates in the Side Letter, the escrow release dates and the TSA Effective Date should all be updated.
2. **Escrow Agent position.** Do we know whether Lanterwick itself asked for Delaware law and forum, or whether Seller's counsel inserted it? This affects whether the split-clause fallback in Issue 4 is needed.
3. **Side Letter rationale.** Has Reitaisk explained why it wants the tax survival change? Was it raised at the business level or traded for anything?
4. **TSA scale and duration.** What share of Cobbelly's airline volume will be produced at Milwaukee under the TSA, and for how long (Schedule A)? This drives how hard to push on the cap and insurance points in Issue 1.
5. **Competitor concerns.** Is the client aware of any planned sale of the Milwaukee Commissary or of Reitaisk's catering operations, or any affiliation with a competing caterer? This would sharpen the assignment point in Issue 5.

Once the client confirms the business points flagged above, I can turn these into a markup of the Escrow Agreement and TSA and a short rejection response on the Side Letter.

## II. Issues (in priority order)

### Issue 1: TSA makes Trouseind an uncapped insurer of Reitaisk's own negligence

**Location:** TSA § 8.1 (Indemnification by Recipient), read with § 8.2 (Indemnification by Provider) and § 9.2 (Cap).

**What the documents say**

- **§ 8.1.** Trouseind, as Recipient, must indemnify, defend and hold harmless the Provider Indemnitees. The indemnity covers "all Losses arising out of or relating to the provision or receipt of the Services, *including any negligence of Provider*." The only carve-out is Losses that Provider must indemnify under § 8.2.
- **§ 8.2.** Provider's indemnity reaches only Losses from Provider's **gross negligence or willful misconduct**.
- **§ 9.2.** Each party's aggregate liability is capped at the TSA Fees, "*other than Article VIII obligations*." The § 8.1 indemnity is therefore uncapped.
- **§ 9.1.** The consequential-damages exclusion does not apply to amounts payable to third parties under Article VIII.

**Why it matters for Trouseind**

- Reitaisk will produce meals for Cobbelly's airline customers at its own Milwaukee Commissary throughout the Service Period. The most likely loss events are contamination, foreign-object, temperature or undeclared-allergen incidents. Each could bring:
  - passenger injury claims;
  - airline customer claims;
  - recall costs; and
  - regulatory penalties.
- If Reitaisk's staff are *ordinarily* negligent in causing such an incident, the loss sits with Trouseind. It falls outside § 8.2, because that clause requires gross negligence. It falls inside § 8.1, because that clause expressly covers Provider negligence.
- The § 8.1 liability has no cap.
- New York courts enforce an indemnity for the indemnitee's own negligence where the intent is unmistakably clear from the contract language. An express reference to "any negligence of Provider" is about as clear as drafting gets. We should assume a court would enforce it as written.
- The structure is backwards for a TSA. Reitaisk controls the kitchen, the personnel (§ 2.5) and the food safety program (§ 2.3). Trouseind has no operational control over production.
- It also undercuts the SPA. Reitaisk gives a Food Safety representation in SPA § 3.17, and the TSA requires Reitaisk to carry product and recall insurance (TSA § 7.1). The § 8.1 indemnity would effectively let Reitaisk's insurers subrogate against, or tender to, Trouseind.

**Recommended fix**

1. Delete "including any negligence of Provider" from § 8.1. Limit Recipient's indemnity to Losses arising from:
   - Recipient's (or the Company's) own negligence or willful misconduct; or
   - Recipient's breach of the TSA, such as inaccurate Customer Specifications supplied by Recipient.
2. Expand § 8.2 so that Provider indemnifies for:
   - Provider's **negligence** (not only gross negligence);
   - breach of §§ 2.2, 2.3 and 2.4;
   - violation of Food Safety Laws; and
   - any product liability, contamination, allergen or recall Losses arising from meals produced at the Milwaukee Commissary.
3. Revise § 9.2 so that Recipient's indemnity is subject to the Fees cap. If any uncapped carve-out survives, it should cover only Provider's food-safety indemnity, and possibly breach of Article VI.
4. Add an express statement that Provider's indemnity is not limited by, and sits alongside, the TSA § 7.1 insurance requirements.

**Business decision for the client:** Trouseind should decide how far it is willing to share production risk during the transition. Reitaisk may argue that the TSA is priced at cost. If so, a middle ground is a mutual negligence-based indemnity with a higher cap for Provider's food-safety indemnity (for example, tied to the $10M umbrella limit). Accepting an uncapped indemnity for the counterparty's own negligence should not be an option.

---

### Issue 2: Escrow Agreement strips Tax and Food Safety claims from the $3,000,000 Extended Holdback

**Location:** Escrow Agreement § 1.1 (definition of "Fundamental Representation Claims") and § 5.3 (Extended Holdback Amount). Compare SPA § 1.1 ("Seller Fundamental Representations"), § 2.4, § 9.6(b) and § 11.10.

| SPA | Escrow Agreement |
|---|---|

| § 2.4: the $3,000,000 Extended Holdback secures breach of the Seller Fundamental Representations *and* Pre-Closing Taxes under § 9.2(c). | § 5.3(a): the Extended Holdback is available "**solely** for Fundamental Representation Claims". The Escrow Agent "shall not disburse any portion... to Buyer for any other Claim." |

**Why it matters for Trouseind**

- Under SPA § 11.10, the Escrow Agreement governs disbursement of the Escrow Funds, so the narrower escrow definition controls.
- Escrow § 6.1 says the Escrow Agent is not bound by or charged with notice of the SPA. Lanterwick will apply the escrow definition literally.
- After the 12-month Initial Release Date, the General Escrow Amount is released. From then on, the only security left is the $3.0M Extended Holdback, and it would cover only organization, authority and capitalization claims. The following would no longer be secured:
  - claims under § 3.14 (Taxes);
  - claims for Pre-Closing Taxes under § 9.2(c); and
  - claims under § 3.17 (Food Safety).
- These are the two risk areas most likely to surface late in an airline catering target: tax audits and latent food-safety or regulatory matters.
- Trouseind would have to pursue Reitaisk directly as an unsecured creditor. That defeats the commercial purpose of the three-year holdback negotiated in SPA § 2.4.

**Recommended fix**

1. Redefine "Fundamental Representation Claims" in Escrow § 1.1 by cross-reference: "Claims for any inaccuracy in or breach of any Seller Fundamental Representation (as defined in the Purchase Agreement) **and any Claim under Section 9.2(c) of the Purchase Agreement**." A cross-reference avoids future drift between the two documents.
2. Conform § 5.1(a), so that the Claim Notice identifies whether a Claim falls in this expanded category, and § 5.3(b).
3. Consider narrowing the SPA § 11.10 carve-out so that the Escrow Agreement governs only the *mechanics* of disbursement. Questions of *which claims* each escrow tranche secures should be governed by the SPA. This is belt-and-braces protection.

This should be a non-controversial conforming change. Reitaisk agreed the substance in SPA § 2.4.

### Issue 3: Side letter cuts tax survival to nine months, ending before Seller's 2026 return is due

**Location:** Seller side letter dated February 20, 2026, § 2 (§ 2.1 replaces SPA § 9.1(b); § 2.3 fixes the Closing Date by reference to SPA § 3.1(c)).

**What the documents say**

- **Current SPA.** SPA § 9.1(b) provides that the § 3.14 Tax representations and the § 9.2(c) Pre-Closing Taxes indemnity survive until **60 days after expiration of the applicable statute of limitations**, giving effect to any waiver or extension.
- **Side letter.** The side letter would replace that with survival "until the date that is **nine (9) months after the Closing Date**."
- **Closing Date.** The target Closing Date is **March 31, 2026** (SPA § 3.1(c); side letter § 2.3). Nine months from that date is **December 31, 2026**.
- **Seller's tax filing obligation.** Under SPA § 6.8(a), Seller files the Seller Group's consolidated federal income Tax Return for the year ending **December 31, 2026**. That return includes the Company through the Closing Date and must be filed by its due date (including extensions). It is not due until **April 15, 2027**, or **October 15, 2027** if extended.

**Why it matters for Trouseind**

- Under the side letter, survival would expire **before the return covering the Company's final pre-closing stub period is even filed**. It would also expire years before the IRS or state authorities could audit and assess any deficiency. The normal federal limitations period is three years from filing, and longer in some cases.
- The exposure is not limited to the stub period. Pre-Closing Taxes include the Company's several liability under Treas. Reg. § 1.1502-6 for every consolidated year of the Seller Group since 2019 (SPA § 3.14(e); "Pre-Closing Taxes" clause (b)). Those years remain open well beyond December 31, 2026.
- In practical terms, Trouseind would lose all meaningful tax indemnity protection.
- The side letter would also hollow out the Extended Holdback, even after Issue 2 is fixed. The holdback runs to the third anniversary, but tax claims would be time-barred after nine months.
- SPA § 9.1(d) preserves claims noticed within the survival period. That does not help, because deficiencies will not be known by December 31, 2026.
- The letter is styled as an SPA § 11.6 amendment, so it would bind once countersigned. It is marked as an unsigned Seller draft "subject to Buyer review" and "not binding unless and until executed," so Trouseind is free to reject it.

**Recommended fix**

- **Reject the side letter** and keep SPA § 9.1(b) as drafted.
- If Reitaisk needs a concession, offer one of the following without sacrificing statute-based survival:
  - a cap on Pre-Closing Tax claims at the Purchase Price (already in SPA § 9.5);
  - enhanced Seller participation rights in tax contests (SPA § 6.8(d)); or
  - a fixed outside date measured from the *later* of the statute of limitations and the filing of the final Seller Group return, in place of the "60 days after" construct.
- Under no circumstances should survival end before the statute of limitations on the 2026 consolidated return, and the pre-2026 consolidated years, has run.

**Business decision for the client:** Ask whether the client wants to treat this as a firm "no" or to use it as a trading chip. Our recommendation is a firm no on the nine-month period itself.

### Issue 4: Escrow Agreement uses Delaware law and an exclusive Chancery forum, splitting Trouseind's recovery

**Location:** Escrow Agreement § 10.2 (Governing Law; Jurisdiction), with the cross-references in § 1.1 ("Final Order"), § 6.5 and § 8.3. Compare SPA § 11.8 (New York law), § 11.9 (exclusive New York County forum, expressly including Transaction Document disputes) and § 11.10.

**What the documents say**

- **Escrow § 10.2** applies "the laws of the State of Delaware." It gives the "Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware" exclusive jurisdiction over any proceeding relating to the Escrow Agreement, expressly including "any dispute concerning the disbursement of, or entitlement to, the Escrow Funds, including whether a Claim is valid."
- **Escrow "Final Order."** A "Final Order" must come from a court with jurisdiction under § 10.2.
- **SPA §§ 11.8 and 11.9.** The SPA and every other Transaction Document are subject to New York law and the New York County courts.
- **TSA § 13.2–13.3.** The TSA is consistent with the SPA on law and forum. The Escrow Agreement is the outlier.

**Why it matters for Trouseind**

- Because SPA § 11.10 lets the Escrow Agreement govern disbursement, Reitaisk can argue that the Delaware clause controls any escrow fight.
- Contested claims are paid only on Joint Written Instructions or a Final Order (Escrow § 5.1(d)). If Reitaisk objects to a Claim, Trouseind could face:
  - litigating Seller's breach and indemnity liability in New York under New York law; and
  - separately litigating "whether a Claim is valid" and entitlement to the funds in Delaware under Delaware law.
- The result would be duplicative cost, a risk of inconsistent rulings, and delay in reaching the cash.
- The "whether a Claim is valid" language is the most troublesome part. It invites Delaware to decide the merits of indemnity claims that the SPA sends to New York.

**Recommended fix**

1. Conform Escrow § 10.2 to SPA §§ 11.8–11.9: New York law, and the exclusive jurisdiction of the state or federal courts in New York County.
2. Delete the "whether a Claim is valid" language. Alternatively, state expressly that the validity and amount of any Claim are determined under the SPA in the New York County courts, and that a final judgment from those courts constitutes a Final Order.
3. Confirm that the interpleader and successor-agent petitions (§§ 6.5, 8.3) also lie in New York County.

Lanterwick may prefer its standard form. Most national escrow agents accept New York law and forum, and New York is commonly used for escrow arrangements, so this should be readily obtainable.
